name: Muscular Dystrophies and Other Muscle Diseases

clinicalPearls: Most myopathies cause persistent, symmetric, proximal (limb-girdle) weakness with preserved reflexes and intact sensation; associated sensory loss instead points toward a peripheral neuropathy or CNS (myelopathy) process rather than primary muscle disease.

The pattern of muscle involvement is the single most useful clue for narrowing the differential: facial weakness with scapular winging suggests FSHD, facial/distal weakness with grip myotonia is virtually diagnostic of myotonic dystrophy type 1, ptosis/ophthalmoparesis suggests oculopharyngeal dystrophy or mitochondrial myopathy, and asymmetric flexor-forearm plus quadriceps weakness suggests inclusion body myositis.

Creatine kinase (CK) is the most sensitive marker of muscle damage; the MM isoenzyme predominates in skeletal muscle while CK-MB marks cardiac muscle. CK can be elevated in healthy people after strenuous activity, trauma, prolonged cramp, or seizure.

Elevated AST, ALT, aldolase, and LDH can originate from muscle and be misattributed to liver disease; a normal gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT) helps confirm a muscle (rather than hepatic) source because GGT is not present in muscle.
The Gower sign (using the arms to climb up the legs to rise from the floor) and a waddling or hyperlordotic toe-walking gait reflect proximal hip, thigh, and trunk weakness.

Calf enlargement in many limb-girdle dystrophies represents true muscle hypertrophy that stays strong late in the disease, so the term 'pseudohypertrophy' is best avoided; by contrast, early medial gastrocnemius atrophy characterizes Miyoshi myopathy (dysferlin/anoctamin-5).

Cardiac and ventilatory muscle involvement are the leading causes of mortality across the dystrophies, so cardiology follow-up, ECG monitoring, and surveillance for respiratory insufficiency are central to care.

Genetic testing is the gold standard for hereditary myopathies, but next-generation panels can miss large deletions/duplications and intronic mutations and frequently return variants of uncertain significance; muscle imaging (MRI/ultrasound) can support a specific diagnosis by showing characteristic involvement patterns.

Myotonic dystrophy type 1 is multisystem: hatchet facies, frontal balding, distal weakness, cataracts, cardiac conduction block, insulin resistance, gonadal atrophy, hypersomnia, and cognitive impairment; congenital DM1 occurs almost exclusively in infants of affected mothers.

Episodic weakness beginning after age 25 is almost never due to a periodic paralysis, with thyrotoxic periodic paralysis being the notable exception (favoring men of Asian descent despite higher thyrotoxicosis rates in women).

In McArdle disease, a slow warm-up or brief rest produces a 'second-wind' phenomenon as the muscle shifts to fatty acid utilization; the forearm exercise test shows a blunted venous lactate rise with a normal ammonia rise.
Ragged red fibers and cytochrome-oxidase (COX)-negative fibers on muscle biopsy, often with elevated serum lactate, FGF-21, and GDF-15, point toward a mitochondrial myopathy.
harrison.pathophysiology: Myopathies reflect structural or functional impairment intrinsic to muscle, distinguishing them from anterior horn cell, peripheral nerve, and neuromuscular junction disorders. In the dystrophies, the molecular defect lies in proteins linking the sarcolemma to the cytoskeleton and extracellular matrix: dystrophin (DMD/BMD) connects the actin cytoskeleton through the dystroglycan complex to the matrix, and mutations in sarcoglycans, dysferlin, calpain-3, anoctamin-5, glycosylation enzymes of alpha-dystroglycan, and sarcomeric/Z-disk and nuclear-envelope proteins underlie the limb-girdle, distal, and Emery-Dreifuss phenotypes. Nuclear-membrane protein defects (emerin, lamin A/C, nesprin-1/2, LUMA) destabilize the inner nuclear envelope and cause EDMD with prominent contractures and arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy. Myotonic dystrophies arise from non-coding repeat expansions (CTG in DMPK for DM1, CCTG in CNBP for DM2) acting through a toxic RNA gain of function: mutant RNA forms nuclear inclusions that sequester splicing regulators, causing widespread aberrant splicing and the multisystem phenotype, with anticipation as repeat length grows across generations. FSHD results from hypomethylation at 4q35 (contracted D4Z4 repeats in FSHD1; SMCHD1/DNMT3B/LRIF1 mutations in FSHD2) that permits toxic expression of the DUX4 transcription factor. Energy-metabolism disorders impair glycolysis (e.g., myophosphorylase/McArdle), glycogen handling (acid maltase/Pompe), or fatty-acid transport into mitochondria via carnitine palmitoyltransferase, producing either exertional cramping with rhabdomyolysis/myoglobinuria or progressive weakness. Mitochondrial myopathies stem from maternally inherited mtDNA point mutations or deletions, or nuclear-gene defects of mtDNA maintenance/replication, impairing oxidative phosphorylation. Channelopathies of the sarcolemma (calcium CACNA1S, sodium SCN4A, potassium Kir2.1, chloride CLCN1) disturb membrane excitability to produce periodic paralysis and/or myotonia. Endocrine and toxic myopathies act through hormonal or pharmacologic injury, often producing fiber atrophy rather than destruction.
additionalDifferentials: Anterior horn cell disease (amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, spinal muscular atrophy)
Myelopathy and other CNS lesions causing weakness
Neuromuscular junction disorders (myasthenia gravis, Lambert-Eaton, congenital myasthenia, botulism)
Inflammatory myopathies (polymyositis, dermatomyositis, immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy, inclusion body myositis)
Fibromyalgia and polymyalgia rheumatica (pain without true weakness; normal CK/EMG/biopsy)
infectionMimics: Pyomyositis and other bacterial muscle infections causing focal muscle enlargement
Parasitic muscle infection (e.g., causing muscle enlargement)
SLONM occurring in the setting of HIV infection
Viral or bacterial infection-triggered episodes of rhabdomyolysis/myoglobinuria
nonInfectiousMimics: Immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy mimicking limb-girdle dystrophy clinically and histopathologically (screen for anti-HMGCR and anti-SRP antibodies)
Sarcoid granulomatous infiltration or amyloid deposition producing muscle enlargement
Hepatic disease wrongly inferred from muscle-derived transaminase/aldolase/LDH elevations
Thyrotoxic hyperreflexia with fasciculations mimicking amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
Diabetic muscle infarction presenting as acute painful indurated thigh/calf swelling
additionalInvestigations: Serum CK (MM vs CK-MB isoenzymes); AST, ALT, aldolase, LDH with GGT to localize muscle vs liver origin

Needle EMG (short-duration small-amplitude polyphasic MUAPs firing early; myotonic discharges; irritability in active necrosis), nerve conduction studies, repetitive nerve stimulation, and single-fiber EMG
Skeletal muscle MRI/ultrasound to define involvement pattern and guide biopsy site
Targeted/next-generation genetic testing (gold standard for hereditary myopathies), with awareness of missed large deletions/intronic mutations and variants of uncertain significance
Muscle biopsy with histochemistry, immunohistochemistry (dystrophin, sarcoglycans, dysferlin, emerin, alpha-dystroglycan) and electron microscopy
Forearm exercise test (lactate and ammonia) for glycolytic defects; dried blood spot enzyme assay screening for Pompe disease
Serum lactate, FGF-21, and GDF-15 for mitochondrial disease; serum/urine potassium and thyroid studies for periodic paralyses; ECG for conduction disease across dystrophies
Endocrine workup: thyroid function tests, parathyroid hormone, vitamin D and calcium; autoantibody panels (including anti-HMGCR, anti-SRP, anti-GAD for stiff-person syndrome)
redFlags: Cardiac conduction abnormalities or arrhythmias (atrial fibrillation, atrioventricular/complete heart block, atrial standstill) in EDMD and myotonic dystrophy carrying risk of sudden death
Dilated cardiomyopathy or heart failure in DMD/BMD, LGMD, and myofibrillar myopathies
Ventilatory/diaphragmatic muscle weakness causing respiratory insufficiency (may be the presenting feature in adult Pompe disease and LGMD)
Myoglobinuria with CK rising to over 100 times normal, signaling rhabdomyolysis
Life-threatening hypokalemia-related arrhythmias during hypokalemic periodic paralysis attacks; potentially serious long-QT and ventricular arrhythmias in Andersen-Tawil syndrome
Dysphagia with aspiration risk in oculopharyngeal dystrophy/OPDM and myotonic dystrophy
Complete heart block and cardiac arrest in Kearns-Sayre syndrome; stroke-like episodes in MELAS
harrison.prognosis: The dystrophies generally follow a slowly progressive course, though severity varies between and within subtypes. Life expectancy is reduced in DMD and BMD, with most BMD patients surviving into the fourth or fifth decade; death is often attributable to associated cardiomyopathy. FSHD usually spares the heart, but about 20% of patients progress to pelvic-girdle involvement and possible wheelchair dependence. In Kearns-Sayre syndrome, death from heart block occurs in roughly 20% of patients, underscoring the value of cardiac surveillance and prophylactic pacing for conduction defects. MELAS in full expression can lead to dementia, a bedridden state, and a fatal outcome. Most endocrine myopathies respond to treatment of the underlying disorder. For many hereditary myopathies no specific disease-modifying therapy exists, and care centers on preserving function and managing cardiac and respiratory complications.
pitfalls: Attributing isolated fatigue to primary muscle disease: fatigue without abnormal clinical or laboratory findings almost never indicates a myopathy, and asthenia must be distinguished from true pathologic fatigability.
Misreading muscle-derived transaminase/aldolase/LDH elevations as liver disease; checking GGT clarifies the source.
Diagnosing myositis in FSHD when biopsy shows an inflammatory infiltrate, leading to incorrect immunosuppressive treatment.
Overlooking immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy (a treatable autoimmune cause) in apparent LGMD without an identified pathogenic mutation; antibody screening is warranted.
Calling calf enlargement 'pseudohypertrophy' when it is true hypertrophy in many LGMDs.
Assuming hyperkalemia in hyperkalemic periodic paralysis; patients are often normokalemic during attacks, and the disorder is defined by precipitation with potassium loading.
Misattributing exertional cramps: cramps follow short intense bursts in glycolytic defects, whereas CPT2-deficiency pain appears only after prolonged exercise once muscle breakdown has begun.
Preferring muscle biopsy over imaging in suspected diabetic muscle infarction, where hemorrhage into the biopsy site can occur.
Relying solely on next-generation sequencing panels, which can miss large deletions/duplications and intronic mutations and may yield variants of uncertain significance.
harrison.severityClassification: No single unifying grading system; severity is assessed disease-specifically. Functional milestones (Gower sign, gait pattern, ambulatory status, wheelchair dependence) and manual muscle testing (e.g., biopsy is best taken from a muscle around grade 4/5) gauge weakness. Mortality risk is stratified by cardiac (conduction disease, cardiomyopathy) and respiratory (ventilatory insufficiency) involvement. In rhabdomyolysis, CK over 100 times normal accompanies myoglobinuria, and for statin myotoxicity, marked CK elevation (more than 3 to 5 times baseline) with severe myalgia, weakness, or myoglobinuria is an indication to stop the drug.
management: Disease-specific therapy where available, including corticosteroids to prolong ambulation in Duchenne muscular dystrophy, mutation-targeted exon-skipping antisense oligonucleotides for eligible genotypes, and enzyme replacement for Pompe disease

Cardiac surveillance and treatment of the associated cardiomyopathy and arrhythmias with ACE inhibitors and beta-blockers, and pacing or defibrillator implantation in Emery-Dreifuss and myotonic dystrophy
Respiratory monitoring with spirometry and overnight oximetry, and non-invasive ventilation for nocturnal hypoventilation
Physiotherapy, stretching and orthoses to prevent contractures, with orthopaedic management of scoliosis
Multidisciplinary neuromuscular care coordinating physiotherapy, occupational therapy, dietetics and respiratory and cardiac specialists
Genetic counselling and family screening for the relevant inheritance pattern, including cardiac assessment of female DMD and BMD carriers
Precautions against malignant-hyperthermia-type anaesthetic reactions and rhabdomyolysis with certain agents, with vigilance for acute deterioration
